text:
Verses 1–8

This chapter of the Qurʾan is focused purely on divine threats and warnings, save for its final two verses that contain glad tidings of paradise and nearness to their Lord for the Godwary.

The chapter begins by calling attention to the miraculous splitting of the moon brought about by the Prophet at the demands of his people. It mentions that they accused him of being a magician, they denied his prophethood, and followed their own desires in spite of the dire warnings he brought to them about the Day of Judgement and the fates of past nations that had perished due to God’s punishment. Then, God calls attention to these accounts in a wrathful and reproachful tone and foretells the evil fate that awaits them on the Day of Resurrection when they are brought forth from their graves and mustered for the final judgement.

Then, the chapter turns to the story of the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, Lot, and Pharaoh and the terrible punishments that befell them because they denied the warnings they were given, before saying that the people of the Prophet are no mightier in relation to God than they had been and have no power to thwart God’s will. The chapter concludes by giving glad tidings to the faithful.

Based on the tone and context of its verses, this chapter is of Meccan provenance. The theory that it was revealed at Badr should be discounted, as should the theory that some of its verses were revealed in Medina. Some of its most beautiful verses are the signs of God’s power invoked towards its end.

(54:1) The Hour has drawn near (iqtarab) and the moon is split The verb iqtarab means to become extremely close. Therefore, when God says, the Hour has drawn near, He means that it is imminent indeed. The Hour is, of course, the time at which the Resurrection takes place.

… and the moon is split: Meaning, that it has been separated into two parts, as indicated. This verse refers to the miraculous splitting of the moon that God caused to happen at the hand of His Prophet in Mecca before the Emigration in response to the demands of the Meccan idolaters. There are abundant narrations that detail this, and both the scholars of traditions and Qurʾanic commentary are in agreement about their authenticity. None of them have differed in this regard except al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ, and al-Balkhī, who have argued that and the moon is split refers to the moon splitting when the Hour sets in. They say that this sentence is phrased in the past tense to show the certainty with which it will occur.

However, this view is bogus and refuted by the contents of the subsequent verse, If they see a sign, they turn away, and say, ‘An incessant magic!’ (54:2), and

its context is the clearest evidence that the term sign here is general in meaning, referring to any miracle, and includes the splitting of the moon. However,

when this occurs, the idolaters turn away and say: ‘An incessant magic!’ This is obviously not something they can say on the Day of Resurrection, the day on which all realities become manifest and humankind will pursue knowledge in order to seek refuge in it. On that day, it would be meaningless for them to say that the splitting of the moon was ‘incessant magic.’ Therefore, there is no other possibility save that this was a miracle that occurred to show the truth and veracity of the Prophet’s claims but that, when it was shown to them, they accused him of practicing magic out of their obstinate disbelief. Equally incorrect is the view that says the verse is a reference to the recent claims of scientists that the moon was originally a part of the earth and the earth was originally part of the sun, and that each of these split of  from the other. According to them, the phrase, the moon is split is a reference to this scientific fact that was unknown to people at the time of revelation. However, even if this theory is correct, it does not accord with the subsequent verse about the reaction of the idolaters, If they see a sign, they turn away, and say, ‘An incessant magic!’ as none of them are recorded as saying that the moon itself was an incessant magic. M oreover, this scientific theory talks about the moon becoming separated from the earth, while the verse is talking about the moon itself splitting into two, as the verb inshiqāq is only used when something splits apart by itself, not when it becomes separated from something

else having previously been a part thereof.

Another incorrect view is the claim that the splitting of the moon refers to the darkness being banished when it rises, and still another is the claim that the splitting of the moon is a metaphor for the truth becoming manifest and God’s command being triumphant.

Moreover, the verse hints subtly at the fact that the splitting of the moon is an inevitable part of the Hour drawing near.

(54:2) If they see a sign (āya), they turn away, and say, ‘An incessant magic (siḥr mustamirr)!’

The adjective mustamirr (incessant) is derived from istimrār, which means for something to go on and on continuously without stopping. Therefore, it is used for something that does not cease. Therefore, ‘An incessant magic’ means that there has been one magic trick after another.

Here, the word āya (sign) is indefinite, which conveys a sense of generality and gives it the meaning of ‘every sign that they witness, they claim it is

just another magic trick. Some have said that the adjective mustamirr can also mean ‘permanent’ or ‘stable’, others interpret it as meaning ‘ephemeral’ or ‘fieeting’, and others still argue that it means ‘repugnant’ or ‘offensive.’ However, all of these interpretations are far from the term’s apparent meaning.

(54:3) They denied, and followed their own desires, and every matter has a setting

What did they deny? The end of the verse suggests that it was the Prophet and the signs that he brought. In other words, ‘they denied the Prophet and the signs that he brought them, when the fact is that every matter has a place in which it will settle, and then it will be known whether it is true or false, veracious or deceitful. Then, they will know whether the Prophet spoke the truth or not, and whether he was upon the truth or not.’ Therefore, the phrase every matter has a setting should be understood in the same vein as the verse, and you will surely learn its tidings in due time (38:88).

Some have said that what they denied was, in fact, the splitting of the moon. Therefore, the meaning of the verse is: ‘They denied the splitting of the moon and followed their own desires.’ However, the end of the verse, and every matter has a setting, does not accord with this meaning at all.

(54:4) There have already come to them reports containing admonishment (muzdajar)

The term muzdajar is an M-infinitive (maṣdar mīmī) that means to caution someone, these reports (anbāʾ) are either the accounts of earlier nations

whom God destroyed or prophecies about the Day of Resurrection—both interpretations are equally possible. The fact that the verse is followed by reports about the Day of Resurrection then reports about a number of nations who perished as a result of divine punishment suggests that the phrase reports containing admonishment, in fact, refers to both of these meanings simultaneously.

(54:5) far-reaching wisdom (ḥikma bāligha); but warnings are of no avail!

Ḥikma (‘wisdom’) signifies a true statement that is also beneficial, while the adjective bāligha (‘far-reaching’) is derived from bulūgh, which literally means for something to arrive at its destination, but can also be used figuratively to denote the fullness or perfection of a thing. Therefore, far-reaching

wisdom means complete and perfect wisdom that is without deficiency or deficit, whether in of its own self or with regard to its effect.

…but warners (nudhur) are of no avail! The word nudhur is the plural of nadhīr, meaning either ‘someone who brings a warning’ or ‘warning’ in the abstract sense. However, it is the first meaning that is more easily understood in this context.

Therefore, the meaning of the verse is: This Qurʾan (or the message to which they are being called) is far-reaching wisdom, but they denied it and followed their own desires, so what avail are warners or warnings?

(54:6) So turn away from them (fa tawalla ʿanhum)! The day when the Caller calls to a dire thing

The fa in fa tawalla shows that this command is based on the description of their state given above. In other words: ‘Given that they deny your

prophethood and follow their own desires, no amount of warnings will avail them nor will any amount of admonition effect them, so turn away from them and do not repeat your call to them.’

The day when the Caller calls to a dire thing (shayʾ nukur)—al-Rāghib says: ‘Inkār (denial) is the opposite of ʿirfān (acknowledgement). One might say ankartu kadhā (‘I deny such and such’) or nakartu (‘I deny it’). In its original sense, it means that something enters the heart that the heart does not recognise, and this is a kind of ignorance. The Qurʾan says (about Abraham), But when he saw their hands not reaching for it, he took them amiss (11:70). The word nukur can also mean ‘cleverness’ or something that is difficult to comprehend.’

The phrase, So turn away from them is the final word on the state of the deniers in relation to the far-reaching wisdom that has been presented to them and the admonitions addressed to them as a warning. Then God repeated some of these admonitions, which are accounts of what their condition will be on the Day of Resurrection and the fates of those earlier nations who denied their prophets. In doing so, He employs a harshly rebuking tone that inspires fear in the hearts in order to grab their attention and deprive them of any excuses, to justify His command to His Prophet to turn away from them.

Therefore, the phrase, The day when the Caller calls, is a new statement, separate from what came before it— as indicated by the previously mentioned admonitions—and it is phrased as an answer to a question that is implicit in the command, So turn away from them. So, for instance, someone might ask: ‘What will be become of them?’ The answer is: The day when the Caller calls…— in other words, this will be their condition in their afterlife, this is the

consequence of the worldly lives lived by those like them and those in whose footsteps they follow from the peoples of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, and others, who they are not better than.

Based on this, the adverbial phrase, The day when…, qualifies the verse, they will emerge from the graves… Hence, the meaning is as follows: ‘They will emerge from the graves on the day when the Caller calls to a dire thing…’ Alternatively, it could be read as meaning, ‘And mention the day when the Caller calls…’ In other words, ‘mention that day and their condition on that day…’ This renders the meaning of this verse in the same vein as the verses, Do they await anything but that the Hour should overtake them suddenly, while they are unaware? (43:66) and Do they await anything except the like of the days of those who passed away before them? (10:102).

Why does God not specify the identity of this caller? Elsewhere in the Qurʾan, He has ascribed this call to Himself: The day He calls you, you will respond to Him, praising Him (17:52).

The reason why God describes their experience of the Resurrection here— their being called forth and emerging from their graves with fear and anxiety in their eyes and scrambling towards the one who has summoned them to face their Final Judgement— is to draw a parallel with their being called to faith in this life through God’s signs, which they turn away from and dismiss as ‘incessant magic.’

Therefore, the meaning of the verse is: ‘Recall the day on which the Caller will summon them for an affair that will be difficult for them, namely the judgement and recompense of the Hereafter.’

(54:7) with a humbled look (khushshaʿan abṣāruhum), they will emerge from the graves (ajdāth) as if they were scattered locusts, The word khushshaʿ is the plural of khāshiʿ (‘one who is humbled and fearful’), which is derived from khushūʿ, which denotes a kind of humility. This is attributed to their sights (abṣār) because that is where this fear is most apparent.

Ajdāth (‘graves’) is the plural of jadath, which is synonymous with qabr (‘grave’). They are compared to scattered locusts (jarād muntashir) when emerging from their resting places because when locusts swarm they mix together and crawl over one another in all directions. Those emerging from their graves on the Day of Resurrection will do likewise, as God says in Sūrah al-Maʿārij, the day when they emerge from the graves, hastening, as if racing toward a target, with a humbled look, overcast by abasement. That is the day they had been promised (70:43–44).

(54:8) scrambling toward the summoner. The faithless will say, ‘This is a hard day!’

In other words, while they are all clambering over one another in a rush to respond to the one who has called them forth, the faithless will say, ‘This is a most difficult day!’

Examining Narrations

(1) In Tafsīr al-Qummī, about the verse, The Hour has drawn near (54:1), we read: ‘The Resurrection is imminent, for there is nothing after the Messenger of God except the Resurrection, and both prophethood and messengership have come to an end. As for the verse, and

the moon is split (54:2), the Quraysh had asked the Messenger of God to show them a sign, so he invoked God to split the moon into two halves so that they might see it clearly. But when He did, they said: “An incessant magic!” Meaning “a genuine magic.”’

(2) In the Amālī of Shaykh al-Mufīd, via a chain of narrators from ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿAlī, from Imām al-Riḍā, from his forefathers, from ʿAlī, it is related: ‘In M ecca, the moon split into two parts. W hen this happened, God’s M essenger said, “Bear witness! Bear witness!”’ (3) In al-Durr al-manthūr, ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, ʿAbd b. Ḥumayd, Muslim, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī in his Dalāʾil narrate from Anas: ‘The people of Mecca asked the Prophet for a sign, so he split the moon in twain in Mecca, then the verse was revealed, The Hour has drawn near and the moon is split… say, “An incessant magic!”’

(4) In the same source, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abū Naʿīm, and al-Bayhaqī—both of them in the Dalāʾil—relate via Masrūq from Ibn Masʿūd: ‘The moon split during the time of the Prophet, but the Quraysh said, “This is the sorcery of Ibn Abī Kabsha! Wait and see what word the Safiār tribe bring you, for Muḥammad cannot bewitch all of humankind.” The Safiār tribe came, the people asked them about it, and they said: “Yes, we saw it too!” Whereat God sent down the verse, The Hour has drawn near and the moon is split.’

(5) In the same source, M uslim, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-M undhir, Ibn M ardawah, al-Ḥākim, al-Bayhaqī, and Abū Naʿīm in his Dalāʾil narrate via Mujāhid from Ibn ʿUmar, concerning the verse, The Hour has drawn near and the moon is split: ‘That happened during the time of God’s Messenger. It split into two parts: One in front of the mountain and one behind it. Whereat the Prophet proclaimed: “O God, bear witness!”’

(6) In the same source, Aḥmad, ʿAbd b. Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ḥākim, Abū Naʿīm, and al-Bayhaqī narrate from Jubayr b. Muṭʿim, concerning the verse, the moon is split: ‘The moon split while we were in Mecca during the time of the Messenger of God. It broke into two pieces: One was above this mountain and the other was above that one. People said, “Muḥammad has bewitched us!”

But a man said, “Even if he has bewitched you, he could not bewitch all mankind!”’

(7) In the same source, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abū Naʿīm in the Dalāʾil narrate from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning the verse, The Hour has drawn near and the moon is split: ‘That happened before the Emigration. The moon split such that we could visibly see it in two parts.’

(8) In the same source, Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd b. Ḥumayd, ʿAbd Allāh b. Aḥmad in the Zawāʾidal-zuhd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abū Naʿīm narrate from Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī: ‘Hudhayfa b. al-Yamān delivered a sermon to us in M adāʾin. He praised and magnified God, then said: “The Hour has drawn near and the moon is split”—Lo! Surely the Hour has drawn nigh! Lo! And surely the moon has split during the time of the Messenger of God! Lo! And surely the world has announced its imminent departure! Lo! Surely today is the race track and tomorrow is the race!”

Author’s comments: The splitting of the moon occurred due to the supplication of the Prophet is an event that has been narrated through many different paths from these individuals among the companions, namely Anas, ʿAbd Allah b. Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, Jubayr b. Muṭʿim, Ibn ʿAbbās, Hudhayfa b. al-Yamān. It is mentioned in Rūḥ al-maʿānī that the tradition was narrated by the companions from ʿAlī. It is related by al-Sayyid al-Sharīfiin his commentary on the Mawaqifiand Ibn al-Subkī in his commentary on the Mukhtasar that the tradition is widely transmitted (mutawātir) and there is no doubt concerning its transmission. This is the status of the tradition among the Sunnīs, and

readers will already be well-aware of its status among the Shīʿa.

A Discourse on the Miraculous Splitting of the Moon The Prophet’s miracle of splitting the moon took place in Mecca before the Emigration in response to the demands of the idolaters. This is something accepted by all Muslims without doubt.

The Qurʾan refers to this momentous event in the opening verses of the present chapter, The Hour has drawn near and the moon is split. If they see a sign, they turn away, and say, ‘An incessant magic!’ (54:1–2). The latter of the two verses can only be concerning this event, and suggests that this chapter was revealed shortly after the event it references, because it refers to the fact that the idolaters turned away from this miracle (as they did for all signs and miracles), and derided it as ‘incessant magic.’ This is further confirmed by the abundant traditions and narrations found in both Sunnī and Shīʿī sources concerning the event that are accepted by the scholars of traditions. We have presented some examples of these traditions above.

Therefore, both the Qurʾan and the traditions refer to this event. Now, the splitting of a heavenly body is something that is possible in of itself, and there is nothing rationally impossible about it. As we have already discussed extensively in the first volume of this commentary, supernatural events— such as signs and miracles— are both possible and have actually taken place. One of the clearest pieces of evidence for this is the Qurʾan itself. Therefore it is necessary to accept that this miracle took place, even if this teaching is not part

of the essentials of the religion.

However, some have argued that the manifestation of such a miracle at the hands of the Prophet in response to the demands of the idolaters contradicts the verse, Nothing keeps Us from sending signs except that the ancients denied them. We gave Thamūd the she-camel as an eye-opener, but they wronged her. W e do not send the signs except for deterrence (17:59). One reading of this verse is follows: ‘We do not send such signs to this people, because, when We sent them to earlier peoples, they denied them, and these people are similar in nature to them, so they will likewise deny them. Therefore, there is no point in sending such signs, because they will be inefiective.’ Alternatively, it could be read as saying: ‘We will not send them because We sent them to their predecessors, who denied them, were punished, and perished as a result, and if

we sent such signs to these people, they will likewise deny them, be punished, and perish utterly as well. However, We do not wish to hasten them to punishment. In any case, we will not send the signs to this people like we sent them

to earlier ones.’

Therefore, this verse concerns signs that are sent in respond to people’s demands where these signs do not support a prophet’s claim of divine revelation—as is the case with the Qurʾan and the Prophet’s mission, or Moses’ staf ,

or Jesus’ reviving the dead—or those verses sent down as a grace from God, such as the supernatural powers displayed by the Prophet, which was not in response to any demands from his people.

Alike in meaning to this verse is the verse, Or until you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the sky. And we will not believe your ascension until you bring down for us a book that we may read.’ Say, ‘Immaculate is my Lord! Am I anything but a human, a messenger?’ (17:93).

In order to respond to this objection properly, it is necessary to lay down some preliminaries, namely that the Prophet was sent as the final divine messenger to all the people of this world, as indicated by the verse, Say, ‘O mankind! I am the Messenger of Allah to you all…’ (7:158), and the verse, … and

this Qurʾan has been revealed to me that I may warn thereby you and whomever it may reach (6:19), and the verse, he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets (33:40). And there are other verses besides this.

The Prophet first began his mission in Mecca first by calling its inhabitants and those people who lived nearby to believe in him. In response, they

did their utmost to persecute, abuse, and deride him, ultimately resolving to either expel, imprison, or murder him. Circumstances became sufficiently dangerous that God commanded him to migrate. He had amassed a decent following in M ecca, but most of its inhabitants remained disbelievers, while the

faithful were a minority by comparison and subject to persecution. However, the community was not inconsiderable in size, as evinced by the verse, Have you not regarded those who were told, ‘Keep your hands offfrom fighting, and maintain the prayer…’ (4:77). This shows that some of them had sought permission to fight back against the idolaters, but God had not permitted them

to do so (according to the traditions narrated concerning the occasion of this verses revelation). This shows that they were sufficiently numerous and well equipped to consider an armed response, and they were continuing to grow in numbers.

Then, the Prophet emigrated to Medina and expanded his mission there, spreading Islam amongst the city, the territory surrounding it, the Arab tribes, in Yemen, and throughout the Arabian Peninsula as a whole, save for Mecca and its territory. Then, he extended his mission even beyond the Peninsula by writing letters to the kings and rulers of Persia, Rome, and Egypt in the year 6 A.H.. He captured Mecca in the year 8 A.H., although a number of its inhabitants had already converted to Islam in the eight years between the Prophet’s Emigration and his conquest of the city.

W hen the Prophet passed away, Islam had already spread significantly, but it continued to grow after him, with its message extending to the present day and reaching over one-fifth of the world’s population.

Based on this preamble, we say: The miracle of the splitting the moon was of the category of miracle that was given in response to people’s demands, and which would have occasioned divine punishment were they to deny it. They did deny it and derided it as nothing more than magic. However, God was not about to destroy all of those to whom the Prophet had been sent to—namely the entirety of the world’s population—because not all of them had yet been given conclusive proof of his prophethood. The splitting of the moon took place five years before the Emigration— so that he who perishes might perish by a manifest proof (8:42).

Neither was God about to eradicate all the inhabitants of Mecca and its environs while there were Muslims amongst them, as God says elsewhere, And were it not for faithful men and faithful women, whom you did not know—lest you should trample them, and thus blame for killing them should fall on you unawares; so that Allah may admit into His mercy whomever He wishes. And had they been separate, We would have surely punished the faithless among them with a painful punishment (48:25).

Equally, God was not going to save only the faithful and punish the disbelievers when so many of them would come to believe in the Prophet in the

thirteen years between the splitting of the moon and the conquest of Mecca and all of them would convert—albeit outwardly—following its conquest. This is because neither all nor most of the inhabitants of Mecca and its environs were obstinate or wilful in their disbelief. It was their leaders and rulers who derided the Prophet, persecuted the faithful, and demanded that he show them signs. It is about them that God has said, As for the faithless, it is the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them, they will not have faith (2:6). God warns these obstinate disbelievers on numerous occasions in the Qurʾan that they will be deprived of faith and perish. They did

not believe and God did punish them at the Battle of Badr. Therefore, His predictions came to pass.

Now, if someone were to argue that the verse, Nothing keeps Us from sending signs except that the ancients denied them, is general in scope and, therefore,

negates the possibility of any such miracles being sent, this is incorrect. This is because the verse in question definitely does not apply to miracles being sent in support of a prophet’s claims, such as the Qurʾan—which supported the Prophet’s mission—or the signs sent down as acts of divine grace, such as the supernatural powers manifested by the Prophet, such as giving people information about the Unseen, healing the sick through his supplications, and other such acts.

Now, even if this verse was general in scope, it would only apply to those signs sent in response to demands. Even then, this would only mean that God would not send the signs and miracles demanded by the Quraysh—or that He did not send the Prophet with such miracles—because previous nations had denied them and the Quraysh were of the same nature as them, so they would deny them and this would require God to punish them, but God did not wish to hasten them to punishment.

However, God has clarified why he did not punish the Quraysh in the verse, But Allah will not punish them while you are in their midst, nor will Allah punish them while they plead for forgiveness (8:33). This shows that what prevented God from punishing them was the presence of the Messenger amongst them. This is also highlighted by the verse, They were about to hound you out of the land, to expel you from it, but then they would not have stayed after you but a little (17:76).

Later, He said, W hat excuse have they that Allah should not punish them, when they bar others from the Holy M osque, and they are not its custodians? Its custodians are only the Godwary, but most of them do not know. Their prayer at the House is nothing but whistling and clapping. So taste the punishment because of what you used to defy (8:34–35).

These verses show that there was nothing holding back God’s punishment from the Quraysh other than the presence of the Prophet amongst them. And when this barrier was removed by his departure from Mecca, that was when they tasted God’s punishment in the form of the severe losses they suffered at the Battle of Badr.

Therefore, to sum up, the reason why God would not send signs to them is because the ancients had denied such signs previously, and the Quraysh resembled them in their nature with regards to the obstinate denial of God’s signs.

At the same time, the existence of the Prophet amongst them prevented God from subjecting them to divine punishment. However, once they had committed misdeeds worthy of divine punishment and their protection—in the

form of the presence of the Prophet—had been removed by the Emigration, then there was neither anything to prevent them from being punished nor any reason not to send down a sign in order for the sentence of punishment to become due against them. Therefore, they were punished both for their denial of the sign and for the other punishable misdeeds they had committed, such as baring others from the Holy Mosque and the like thereof.

From this, we can conclude that the verse, Nothing keeps Us from sending signs…, only means that He will not send such signs so long as the Prophet is amongst them. As for sending such signs but delaying the punishment until he is no longer amongst them, there is no indication about this in the verse either way. God has explicitly stated in the Qurʾan that the Battle of Badr was a sign from Him and that what befell the Quraysh in it was a form of divine punishment. The same is true if the verse is read as meaning that God did not send signs to them because they would have no effect on a people who were so committed to denying them. Now, sending such signs and delaying the resulting punishment for their denial until the Prophet was no longer among them would yield the benefit that God may confirm the truth and bring falsehood to naught (8:8). Therefore, the miracle of splitting the moon would be

one of the divine signs whose purpose was to make its recipients deserving of punishment once the Prophet had departed from their midst.

As for the verse, Say, ‘Immaculate is my Lord! Am I anything but a human, a messenger?’ (17:93), it does not preclude God supporting the claims of the Prophet by sending miraculous signs, nor does it deny the possibility of such interventions. On the contrary, it negates the idea that these miracles come from the Prophet himself, insofar as he is a human being and a messenger of God. If it genuinely meant that the Prophet could not perform miracles, this would entail a denial of the miracles of all the prophets, because each and every one of them is ‘a human, a messenger’ and the Qurʾan explicitly contradicts such a denial by virtue of the fact that it is replete with stories of prophets performing miracles. An even clearer contradiction of this is the verse of the Qurʾan that challenges the deniers to produce something equal to it. In fact, what this verse means is that— as a human and a messenger— the Prophet is not capable of producing the miracles the idolaters demand from himself, as this is an affair that is decided by God: If He wishes, He will send down a sign, and if He does not, then He will not. Elsewhere, God says, They swear by Allah with solemn oaths that were a sign to come to them they would surely believe in it. Say, ‘The signs are only with Allah,’ and what will bring home to you that they will not believe even if they came? (6:109).

And about the people of Noah, He says, They said, ‘O Noah, you have disputed with us already, and you have disputed with us exceedingly. Now bring us what you threaten us with should you be truthful.He said, ‘Allah will indeed bring it on you if He wishes, and you cannot thwart’ (11:33).

And He says, A messenger may not bring any sign except by Allah’s permission (40:78).

And there are many other verses in this vein.

Another objection to the miracle of splitting the moon reads as follows: If the moon had split as is claimed, then all of humankind would have seen it. Moreover, astronomers would have recorded the event all over the world, because this would have been a truly momentous celestial event, as nothing like this has come down to us in the books of history or in works dealing with the heavens, when this is certainly something that people would have wanted to record and pass on!

To this, we can respond as follows:

First, we can discount the objection because there is no evidence that every terrestrial or celestial event known to people is recorded by them and handed down from one generation to the next.

Second, the Hejaz, the rest of the Arabian Peninsula, and many of the surrounding lands did not have observatories or professional astronomers. These were found in India to the east and Rome and Greece to the west and other places, but there is no evidence that an observatory existed in the Arabian Peninsula at this time— which, according to some narrations, too place at the beginning of the fourteenth night of Dhū al-Ḥijja, some five years before the Emigration—and this might not have been visible to observers in other lands that were far away from Mecca. Some reports indicate that the moon was a full moon that split at around sunset, when it was just beginning to rise, and it only remained split apart for a very short period of time before joining together again. Therefore, by the time it became visible in lands to the west of Arabia, it would have already returned to its original form.

Another objection is that such a split in the moon could only take place if the gravitational forces holding the two halves together were somehow nullifted, in which case it would be impossible for them to come back together.

Therefore, if the moon split, it would not recombine itself again.

The answer to this is that there is nothing rationally impossible about this taking place. As for this being something unusual, this is the very definition of a miracle. After all, had it been impossible for the two halves to re-join one another, it would have been equally impossible for them to split apart in the first place. However, there is nothing impossible out this, because we have already established that miracles can and do take place.
